name: Magic Link Sign In
description: Passwordless sign-in that says what will land in the inbox and how long it lasts, before the address is typed.

content.heading: Sign in without a password
content.intro: One address, one link, no password to forget or reuse. The link works once and expires in fifteen minutes, which is stated here rather than discovered when it fails.

fields.name: email
fields.label: Email
fields.hint: The link lands here and works once. It expires after 15 minutes.

name: Support Ticket Form
description: A support form that asks for the one thing that halves resolution time — what you already tried — and says when a human will read it.

content.heading: Tell us what broke
content.intro: Most tickets take two round trips because the first reply has to ask what was already tried. This asks up front, and the answer is optional so it never blocks sending.

fields.name: email
fields.label: Email
fields.hint: Where the reply goes. Weekdays, inside four hours.

fields.name: summary
fields.label: What happened?
fields.hint: One sentence. The detail goes below.

fields.name: tried
fields.label: What have you already tried?
fields.hint: Optional, and the field that saves a round trip.

name: Back In Stock Form
description: The capture that replaces a dead sold-out button, with the honest caveat that a notification is not a reservation.

content.heading: Tell me when it is back
content.intro: A sold-out product page with a greyed-out button is a dead end and a lost address. One field turns it into the only useful thing left on the page.

fields.name: email
fields.label: Email
fields.hint: One message when it restocks. This is not a reservation — stock is first come.

fields.name: size
fields.label: Size
fields.hint: Only that size triggers the alert. Leave blank for any.

name: Order Lookup Form
description: Order tracking for the guest who never made an account, which is most of them.

content.heading: Find your order
content.intro: Guest checkout is the majority of orders on most storefronts, and the usual tracking page asks those buyers to sign in to an account they were never offered.

fields.name: order
fields.label: Order number
fields.hint: On the confirmation email, top right. Starts with a #.

fields.name: email
fields.label: Email used at checkout
fields.hint: Both have to match. It is what stops an order number being a lookup key for anyone.

name: Import From URL Form
description: The import path for a file that is already on the internet, which does not need to travel through the browser at all.

content.heading: Import from a link
content.intro: A file that already lives at a URL does not need to be downloaded to a laptop and uploaded again. The server fetches it, which also survives the tab being closed.

fields.name: url
fields.label: File URL
fields.hint: Must be publicly reachable. Signed links work; a login page does not.

fields.name: format
fields.label: Format
fields.hint: Detected from the response, not the extension. Override only if it guesses wrong.

name: Digest Schedule Form
description: The control that turns notification volume down instead of off, which is the choice most people actually want.

content.heading: Send it all at once instead
content.intro: The alternative offered by most products is on or off, so everyone picks off. A time and a floor turns the same stream into one predictable message.

fields.name: time
fields.label: Send at
fields.hint: Your local time. Nothing arrives outside this except an outage.

fields.name: threshold
fields.label: Skip the digest below
fields.hint: Fewer events than this and no message is sent at all. An empty digest is still an interruption.

name: Workspace Setup Form
description: The first screen after signup, asking only the two things that cannot be changed silently later.

content.heading: Name your workspace
content.intro: Everything else in setup has a sensible default and can be changed later without telling anyone. These two appear in URLs and invitations, so they are worth one screen.

fields.name: name
fields.label: Workspace name
fields.hint: Shown to everyone you invite. Changeable at any time.

fields.name: slug
fields.label: URL
fields.hint: Becomes part of every link you share. Changing it later breaks the old ones.

name: Demo Request Form
description: A demo request that offers the self-serve escape first, so the people who did not want a call do not book one.

content.heading: See it on your own data
content.intro: Thirty minutes, screen-shared, against something of yours rather than a seeded demo account. If you would rather not talk to anyone, the free tier is the same product.

fields.name: goal
fields.label: What do you want to see?
fields.hint: One line. It decides what gets set up before you arrive.

name: Gift Options Form
description: The gifting step, placed in the cart where it is a choice rather than at checkout where it is friction.

content.heading: Sending this as a gift?
content.intro: In the cart rather than at checkout, because a gift message added while someone is entering card details is a step between them and paying. Here it is part of choosing.

fields.name: message
fields.label: Message on the card
fields.hint: Handwritten and enclosed. Up to 200 characters.

fields.name: from
fields.label: From
fields.hint: Signed as written. Leave blank to stay anonymous.

name: Context Scope List
description: Which sources this answer may draw on, shown as a scope the user can read before asking rather than a citation list after.

content.heading: What it can see
content.intro: Citations tell you what an answer used. Scope tells you what it could have used, which is the question behind "why did it not know that".

items.label: Public documentation
items.detail: Always in scope. Re-indexed on every deploy.

items.label: Your workspace files
items.detail: In scope. Only files your own account can already open.

items.label: Support ticket history
items.detail: In scope for your organisation's tickets, never another customer's.

items.label: Billing and payment records
items.detail: Out of scope. No retrieval path reaches them, and turning it on is not an option here.

name: Escalation Queue
description: What is waiting on a person, ordered by how long it has been waiting rather than when it arrived.

content.heading: Waiting on a person
content.intro: Sorted by age, not arrival. A queue sorted newest-first buries the item that has been stuck longest, which is always the one that turns into the complaint.

items.label: Refund over the auto-approve limit
items.detail: £840. Two people can sign this and neither has opened it.

items.label: Outbound message to a customer
items.detail: Drafted by the agent, held because the recipient is outside the workspace.

items.label: Schema change on a production table
items.detail: Additive, reversible, and still not something a run should do unattended.

items.label: New integration scope request
items.detail: Read-only calendar access. Expires on its own in two days if nobody acts.

name: Agent Cost Breakdown
description: What one run cost, per step, so an expensive answer is attributable rather than a monthly surprise.

content.heading: What this run cost
content.intro: Per step, not per month. A bill that only arrives in aggregate cannot be acted on — the useful version says which step was expensive and whether it needed to be.

items.label: Retrieval — 12 passages
items.detail: Cheap and worth it. Cutting this is what makes the model guess.

items.label: Reasoning — 4 steps
items.detail: The bulk of it. Three steps would have reached the same answer.

items.label: Tool calls — 6 invocations
items.detail: One retry included, which is billed like any other call.

items.label: Final answer
items.detail: Output tokens only. The cheapest part of almost every run.

name: Inline AI Action Menu
description: The actions offered on a selection, each saying whether it rewrites in place or opens a draft beside it.

content.heading: Do something with the selection
content.intro: Every row says where the result lands. An AI action that silently replaces the paragraph someone spent ten minutes on is the fastest way to have the feature turned off.

items.label: Rewrite for clarity
items.detail: Replaces the selection. One undo puts it back exactly.

items.label: Shorten to one sentence
items.detail: Replaces the selection. Undo restores the original wording.

items.label: Suggest three alternatives
items.detail: Opens beside the text. Nothing changes until one is picked.

items.label: Explain this passage
items.detail: Read-only. Never touches the document.

name: Notification Channel List
description: Which channel carries which event, so the loud ones can be moved rather than muted entirely.

content.heading: Where each thing goes
content.intro: The all-or-nothing toggle is why people mute products. Routing by event lets the two that matter stay loud while the rest go somewhere quiet.

items.label: Production incidents
items.detail: Push and email, immediately, ignoring quiet hours.

items.label: Someone mentions you
items.detail: Push during working hours, batched into the digest outside them.

items.label: Build results
items.detail: Digest only. Failures are already in the incident row above.

items.label: Product announcements
items.detail: Email, monthly, and the unsubscribe link is not buried.

name: Plan Limits List
description: What actually runs out on each plan, including what happens when it does — the row a pricing table leaves off.

content.heading: What runs out, and what happens then
content.intro: Pricing tables list what a plan includes. They rarely say what happens at the limit, which is the thing that decides whether a limit is survivable.

items.label: Seats
items.detail: Hard limit. Inviting past it prompts an upgrade rather than charging silently.

items.label: API requests
items.detail: Soft. You are throttled, not cut off, and told at 80%.

items.label: Storage
items.detail: Soft, then read-only. Nothing is ever deleted for being over.

items.label: Retention
items.detail: Hard. Data past the window is deleted on schedule and cannot be recovered.

name: Metric Alert List
description: Alert thresholds with their current distance from firing, so a quiet alert is visibly armed rather than possibly broken.

content.heading: Alerts, and how close they are
content.intro: An alert that has never fired looks identical to an alert that is broken. Showing the current distance to the threshold is what tells the two apart at a glance.

items.label: Error rate above 1%
items.detail: Currently 0.08%. Fired twice this quarter, both real.

items.label: p95 latency above 800 ms
items.detail: Currently 690 ms and climbing through the week.

items.label: Queue depth above 5,000
items.detail: Currently 4,880. This is the one to look at first.

items.label: Daily signups below 20
items.detail: Currently 74. A floor alert, so under is the safe side.

name: Stock Availability List
description: Availability per variant stated before the cart, because discovering it at checkout is where the basket gets abandoned.

content.heading: What is actually available
content.intro: "In stock" on a listing that means "one of nine variants is in stock" is the single most expensive lie in commerce UI — it is discovered at checkout, and the basket is abandoned there.

items.label: Small — Charcoal
items.detail: Ships today if ordered before 4pm.

items.label: Medium — Charcoal
items.detail: Low. The counter is live, not a scarcity banner.

items.label: Large — Charcoal
items.detail: Restocking. Notify me is on the product page.

items.label: Small — Sand
items.detail: Made to order. Six weeks, stated here rather than at checkout.

name: Recent Search List
description: The empty state of a search box, filled with the searches that are worth repeating and the ones worth saving.

content.heading: Pick up where you left off
content.intro: An empty search box is the most common state of a search box, and it is usually blank. Recent queries are the cheapest useful thing to put there, and the result count is what makes them worth re-running.

items.label: status:open assignee:me
items.detail: Run four times this week. The closest thing you have to a saved view.

items.label: invoice overdue
items.detail: Run yesterday. Two more have gone overdue since.

items.label: "cannot log in"
items.detail: Exact phrase. Quoted searches are kept verbatim rather than re-tokenised.

items.label: region:eu plan:enterprise
items.detail: Returned nothing last time. Kept anyway — an empty result is information.

name: Security FAQ
description: The security questions a buyer's IT reviewer asks, answered with scope and dates rather than with the word "enterprise-grade".

content.heading: Security, answered properly
content.intro: These four arrive in every procurement review. Answering them on a public page rather than in a questionnaire is worth about two weeks of a sales cycle.

items.label: Where is our data stored?
items.detail: The region you pick at signup. It is pinned there and never replicated out of it.

items.label: Do you train models on it?
items.detail: No, and there is no setting that turns it on.

items.label: Who internally can read it?
items.detail: Support, on an approved ticket, time-boxed and logged. You can export that log.

items.label: What happens when we leave?
items.detail: Full export any time. Deletion within 30 days of the request, backups included.

name: Enterprise SSO Split
description: What SSO actually covers, written for the person who has to configure it rather than the person who asked for it.

content.heading: Your directory, your rules
content.intro: SSO on a pricing page is one word. To the person configuring it, it is four separate features that vendors bundle inconsistently — so this names them.

items.label: SAML 2.0 and OIDC
items.detail: Both, against any provider. Okta, Entra and Google are documented step by step.

items.label: SCIM provisioning
items.detail: Users appear and disappear with your directory. Deprovisioning is the half that matters.

items.label: Enforced, not optional
items.detail: Password login can be switched off per domain, so a bypass is not one setting away.

items.label: Included, not an upsell
items.detail: On every paid plan. Charging for the control that makes offboarding safe is a security tax.

name: Data Migration Split
description: What a migration actually moves and what it cannot, stated before the switch rather than discovered after it.

content.heading: We move it, and we say what we cannot
content.intro: Every migration page promises everything comes across. Something never does, and finding out which thing after the cutover is how a switch becomes a rollback.

items.label: Records, history and attachments
items.detail: Everything with a stable id, including the timestamps, so reports still line up.

items.label: Users and their permissions
items.detail: Roles are mapped, and the mapping is shown for approval before anything is written.

items.label: What does not come across
items.detail: Custom automations. The triggers have no equivalent here and a silent half-migration is worse.

items.label: Run it twice
items.detail: A trial into a sandbox first, then the real one. The trial is free and does not count against anything.

name: Integration Depth Split
description: An integrations section that says how deep each one goes, instead of a wall of logos that all imply the same thing.

content.heading: Not all of these mean the same thing
content.intro: A grid of thirty logos implies thirty equivalent integrations. Usually four are deep, six are one-way, and the rest are a Zapier entry. Saying which is which costs one sentence each.

items.label: Two-way sync
items.detail: Changes flow both directions and conflicts are resolved, not last-write-wins.

items.label: One-way import
items.detail: We read from them on a schedule. Nothing is written back, which is often what you want.

items.label: Notifications only
items.detail: We post events into the channel. Honest, useful, and not a sync — so it is not listed as one.

items.label: Via the API
items.detail: Everything else. Documented, versioned, and the same API the first row is built on.

name: Human Oversight Split
description: Where a person sits in an automated run, written as four guarantees rather than as a promise that a human is involved.

content.heading: Where the person actually is
content.intro: "A human is in the loop" is a claim with no shape. These are the four points where one really is, and each is a thing the system will not do without them.

items.label: Before anything leaves
items.detail: External messages and payments stop and wait. The full payload is shown, not a summary of it.

items.label: On low confidence
items.detail: The run pauses rather than picking the best of four bad options and presenting it as an answer.

items.label: After the fact, in the log
items.detail: Every unattended action is recorded with its inputs, and the log is exportable.

items.label: The stop button
items.detail: One press halts a run mid-step and rolls back anything reversible. It is always on screen.

name: Grounding Split
description: How an answer is tied to its sources, and what the system does when it cannot find any.

content.heading: Every claim points at something
content.intro: The interesting half of a retrieval system is not what it does when it finds the answer. It is what it does when it does not.

items.label: Citations on the sentence
items.detail: Not a source list at the bottom. The claim and its evidence are next to each other or the citation is decoration.

items.label: Quoted, not paraphrased
items.detail: The retrieved passage is shown as written, so you can see whether it says what the answer claims.

items.label: It says when it does not know
items.detail: No passage above the relevance floor produces "I could not find this", not a fluent guess.

items.label: Stale sources are flagged
items.detail: Age travels with the passage. A confident answer from a two-year-old document is the failure nobody catches.

name: Collection Story Split
description: The editorial header above a collection grid, carrying the four facts that decide a considered purchase.

content.heading: Made to be repaired, not replaced
content.intro: A grid of forty products with a one-line title is a search result. For anything considered, the reason the collection exists is what does the selling, and it belongs above the grid rather than on a linked story page nobody opens.

items.label: One factory, named
items.detail: Porto, family-run, thirty years. The address is on the about page rather than implied by a photograph.

items.label: Repairs, not warranties
items.detail: Send it back at any age. Repair is charged at cost and typically beats replacing it.

items.label: Deadstock and offcuts
items.detail: Which is why sizes run out and do not come back. The stock list says which.

items.label: Priced once
items.detail: No seasonal markdown, so nobody who bought in March is punished for it in July.

name: Review Distribution Band
description: The rating summary with the numbers that make an average trustworthy — the count, the spread and the verified share.

content.heading: 4.6, and the numbers behind it
content.intro: An average with nothing beside it is unreadable: 4.6 from nine reviews and 4.6 from nine hundred are different facts. These are what make the first number mean something.

items.label: Average
items.detail: Across every review, including the ones left after a return.

items.label: Reviews
items.detail: Unfiltered. Nothing is hidden for being low.

items.label: Verified purchase
items.detail: Matched to an order. The other 9% are labelled as such.

items.label: One and two star
items.detail: Shown, and sorted to the top when you filter by lowest.

name: Customer Outcome Band
description: Testimonials reduced to the measured outcome and the conditions it happened under, for readers who skip the quotes.

content.heading: What changed, and over how long
content.intro: Most readers skip the quotes. What they do not skip is a number with a time period attached to it, and every figure here names the company it came from and how long it took.

items.label: Support replies
items.detail: Median first-response time at Northwind, over one quarter.

items.label: Onboarding
items.detail: Time to a customer's first live workspace, at Arden.

items.label: Manual reconciliation
items.detail: Hours returned to one finance team of three, measured before and after.

items.label: Kept using it
items.detail: Of teams past 90 days, over the last twelve months.

name: KPI Summary Band
description: The top-of-dashboard figures, each carrying the comparison period that makes a delta mean anything.

content.heading: The four numbers the team looks at
content.intro: Every figure names what it is being compared against. A delta with no stated period is the most common way a dashboard misleads the people who built it.

items.label: Active workspaces
items.detail: +7.2% on the previous 30 days, not on last calendar month.

items.label: Net revenue retention
items.detail: Trailing twelve months, expansion minus churn and contraction.

items.label: p95 latency
items.detail: Same period, all regions. p50 is 96 ms and hides this.

items.label: Open incidents
items.detail: Degraded, not down. Public status page has the detail.
